title: Replacement Property Identification
name: Replacement Property Identification
metaTitle: Replacement Property Identification in San Jose, CA
metaDescription: Building a defensible 45-day identification list across San Jose's submarkets, from North San Jose R&D to Almaden, before the exchange clock runs out.

sections.html: The 45-day identification window is short, and San Jose is not a market where you can walk into a corridor cold and expect the right building to be sitting there waiting. We build identification lists by working the submarkets we already know, from the North San Jose research and development campuses down to the quieter Almaden Valley corridor, so a client's list reflects real available inventory rather than a generic search.

sections.heading: Starting the List Before the Relinquished Property Even Closes
sections.html: The 45-day clock starts on the closing date of the relinquished property, not when a client starts thinking about replacements, so we begin building candidate lists as soon as a sale is under contract. That means walking North San Jose's flex and R&D corridor near Component Drive and Trimble Road, checking transit-village multifamily activity around Berryessa BART, and confirming what's actually listed versus what's simply been on a broker's pocket list for months without a real seller behind it.

sections.heading: Choosing Between the Three-Property Rule and the 200 Percent Rule
sections.html: Most San Jose exchanges default to naming three properties without much thought, but the 200 percent rule can be the better fit when a client wants more than three candidates because inventory is thin in a given corridor, like Coyote Valley's slow-moving industrial land or a tight pocket of medical office near a hospital campus. Under the 200 percent rule, any number of properties can be identified as long as their combined value doesn't exceed twice the relinquished property's sale price, which gives more room to hedge against a deal falling through.

sections.heading: Why Backup Candidates Matter More in a Land-Scarce Market
sections.html: Land scarcity across San Jose, especially in North San Jose and the Golden Triangle industrial area, means a single identified property can fall out of contract for reasons that have nothing to do with the buyer, a lender pulling back, a seller getting a better offer elsewhere, a title issue surfacing late. We build every identification list with at least one realistic backup candidate that could close inside the 180-day exchange period if the primary choice fails, rather than leaving a client with no path forward.

sections.heading: What Goes Into a Defensible Identification Notice
sections.html:
A written identification notice delivered to the qualified intermediary within 45 days needs to describe each property unambiguously, typically street address or legal description, and should reflect:

  • Properties actually available and under realistic terms, not aspirational listings
  • A clear choice between the three-property rule and the 200 percent rule based on real inventory
  • At least one backup candidate with a plausible path to closing inside 180 days
  • Ownership structure noted for any condo, ground lease, or fractional interest
  • Confirmation that each property is legally described well enough to satisfy the identification requirement

sections.heading: Scheduling Site Visits Across a Scattered City in a Short Window
sections.html:
San Jose's submarkets don't sit close together, a morning spent walking North San Jose's flex corridor near Component Drive can be an hour or more from an afternoon stop in Almaden Valley or Coyote Valley, and a 45-day window doesn't leave room for wasted trips. We sequence site visits by geography and by which candidates are moving fastest toward a decision from a competing buyer, so the client sees the properties most likely to disappear first.

We also try to schedule a second look at any serious candidate before it's finalized on the list, since a walk-through on a weekday morning can reveal parking congestion or loading conflicts that a Sunday afternoon showing never surfaces.

When a client is juggling a full-time job or a business alongside the exchange, we condense the visit schedule into as few trips as possible and share notes and photos on the properties they can't personally walk through, so the 45-day window doesn't get eaten up by logistics alone.

faqs.q: When does the 45-day identification clock actually start?
faqs.a: It starts on the day the relinquished property closes, not when you first started looking for a replacement, so the sourcing work needs to begin before that closing date if at all possible. Waiting until after closing to start looking almost always compresses the timeline more than clients expect.

faqs.q: Can I change my identified properties after the 45-day deadline?
faqs.a: No, once the 45-day window closes, the identification list is generally locked, which is why we push clients to have realistic backup candidates named from the start rather than hoping to swap in a better option later. Revocation and replacement are only possible within the 45 days themselves.

faqs.q: How many properties can I identify?
faqs.a: Under the three-property rule you can name up to three regardless of value, and under the 200 percent rule you can name more as long as their combined fair market value doesn't exceed twice what you sold. Which rule fits depends on how much real inventory exists in the corridors you're targeting.

faqs.q: What if none of my identified properties end up closing?
faqs.a: If none of the identified properties close within the 180-day exchange period, the exchange fails and the transaction is treated as a taxable sale, which is exactly why backup candidates matter so much in a market where deals fall through for reasons outside your control. We build lists with that risk in mind.

faqs.q: Do you help draft the identification notice itself?
faqs.a: We help assemble the property details and descriptions that go into the notice, but the qualified intermediary is the party who receives it and confirms it satisfies the legal requirements. We coordinate closely with the intermediary so nothing gets missed before the deadline.
